key_concept: Frogs carry out cutaneous respiration: when submerged, gas exchange happens by diffusion across their moist, highly vascularised skin.
steps: Frogs have three respiratory surfaces: skin (cutaneous), buccal cavity (buccopharyngeal) and lungs (pulmonary).
In water the frog cannot breathe air, so its lungs and buccal cavity cannot be ventilated.
Dissolved $O_2$ in the water diffuses across the thin, moist, richly vascularised skin into the blood, and $CO_2$ diffuses out the same way.
This is cutaneous respiration, the only mode used while the frog is submerged (and also during hibernation and aestivation).
On land the frog uses the buccal cavity, the skin and the lungs, with the lungs used mainly during active periods.
So the answer is skin, which matches the official key.
why_not_others: The buccal cavity and lungs take part in respiration only on land, when air is available. Adult frogs have no trachea used as a respiratory organ; tracheal respiration is a feature of insects.
common_trap: Students choose lungs because adult frogs have lungs, forgetting that lungs work only with air on land and not underwater.
time_saving_tip: Remember 'Water → Skin; Land → Skin + Buccal cavity + Lungs' to answer frog respiration questions instantly.
